This page summarizes, extends and updates the seminal PortSwigger research on Browser-Powered Desync Attacks and subsequent work on HTTP/2 connection-state abuse. It focuses on vulnerabilities where an origin is determined only once per TCP/TLS connection , enabling an attacker to âsmuggleâ requests to a different internal host once the channel is established. Connection-State Attacks First-request Validation When routing requests, reverse proxies might depend on the Host (or :authority in HTTP/2) header to determine the destination back-end server, often relying on a whitelist of hosts that are permitted access. However, a vulnerability exists in a number of proxies where the whitelist is only enforced on the very first request in a connection . Consequently, attackers can access internal virtual hosts by first sending an allowed request and then re-using the same underlying connection: GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: allowed-external-host.example GET /admin HTTP/1.1 Host: internal-only.example First-request Routing Many HTTP/1.1 reverse proxies map an outbound connection to a back-end pool based exclusively on the first request they forward . All subsequent requests sent through the same front-end socket are silently re-used, regardless of their Host header. This can be combined with classic Host header attacks such as password-reset poisoning or web cache poisoning to obtain SSRF-like access to other virtual hosts: GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: public.example POST /pwreset HTTP/1.1 Host: private.internal Tip In Burp Suite Professional â¥2022.10 you can enable HTTP Request Smuggler â Connection-state probe to automatically detect these weaknesses. NEW in 2023-2025 â HTTP/2/3 Connection Coalescing Abuse Modern browsers routinely coalesce HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 requests onto a single TLS connection when the certificate, ALPN protocol and IP address match. If a front-end only authorizes the first request, every subsequent coalesced request inherits that authorisation â even if the Host/:authority changes . Exploitation scenario The attacker controls evil.com which resolves to the same CDN edge node as the target internal.company . The victimâs browser already has an open HTTP/2 connection to evil.com . The attacker embeds a hidden in their page. Because the connection parameters match, the browser re-uses the existing TLS connection and multiplexes the request for internal.company . If the CDN/router only validated the first request, the internal host is exposed. PoCs for Chrome/Edge/Firefox are available in James Kettleâs talk âHTTP/2: The Sequel is Always Worseâ (Black Hat USA 2023). Tooling Burp Suite 2023.12 introduced an experimental HTTP/2 Smuggler insertion point that automatically attempts coalescing and TE/CL techniques. smuggleFuzz (https://github.com/microsoft/smugglefuzz) â A Python framework released in 2024 to brute-force front-end/back-end desync vectors over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, including connection-state permutations. Mitigations Always re-validate Host/:authority on every request , not only on connection creation. Disable or strictly scope origin coalescing on CDN/load-balancer layers (e.g. http2_origin_cn off in NGINX). Deploy separate certificates or IP addresses for internal and external hostnames so the browser cannot legally coalesce them. Prefer connection: close or proxy_next_upstream after each request where practical. Real-World Cases (2022-2025) Year Component CVE Notes 2022 AWS Application Load Balancer â Host header only validated on first request; fixed by patching rules engine (disclosed by SecurityLabs). 2023 Apache Traffic Server < 9.2.2 CVE-2023-39852 Allowed request smuggling via HTTP/2 connection reuse when CONFIG proxy.config.http.parent_proxy_routing_enable was set. 2024 Envoy Proxy < 1.29.0 CVE-2024-2470 Improper validation of :authority after first stream enabled cross-tenant request smuggling in shared meshes. Detection Cheat-Sheet Send two requests in the same TCP/TLS connection with different Host or :authority headers. Observe whether the second response originates from the first host (safe) or the second host (vulnerable). In Burp: Repeat â keep-alive â Send â Follow . When testing HTTP/2, open a dedicated stream (ID 1) for a benign host, then multiplex a second stream (ID 3) to an internal host and look for a reply.
